newsitem.title: USA: GRAIN--IRS memo not likely to raise farmer 96 tax.
newsitem.headline: GRAIN--IRS memo not likely to raise farmer 96 tax.

text.p: Concern about possible changes in Internal Revenue Service tax policy on some cash grain deals circulated in farm communities this week but farmers' 1996 tax bills likely won't rise, grain industry sources said.
"It shouldn't affect their marketing strategy," said Tom Husek, accountant with the Illinois Agricultural Auditing Association, adding most farmers would likely be unaffected.
At issue is a December 1995 IRS memo about a Washington state farmer who sold potatoes and received some cash at delivery but deferred some payment until the following year.

The memo, not yet published in the Federal Register and so not part of the official tax code, has been discussed in trade publications as a possible surprise tax for grain farmers, who widely use deferred-payment (DP) contracts to sell crops.
In the potato farmer's case, IRS ruled that the entire income from the sale should be reported under alternative minimum tax (AMT) rules, applicable for the same tax year.

AMT taxes a broader base of income at a lower rate and farmers must pay the AMT if it is higher than normal income tax. Grain farmers have been scrambling to decide whether to avoid DP and store grain until next year, grain dealers said.

But tax specialists contacted by Reuters said the IRS memo leaves a wide grey area when it comes to traditional DP grain contracts as long as the contracts don't involve any payment at the time of delivery, said Dave Miller, commodity policy specialist at the American Farm Bureau Federation.
Most DP contracts in the grain market don't involve up-front payments and farmers normally ask for payment after January 1 anyway, according to several grain merchants.
"It's not clear that simple DP contracts are subject to AMT," Miller said. "Previous rulings tend to indicate that a contract with simply a pledge to pay has no face value."
"It's a big deal for some guys but most of our farmers have not been too concerned about it," said a merchandiser at a central Illinois terminal when asked about the tax issue.
DP contracts were especially popular with farmers this year after corn prices fell sharply from record highs, said Jim Quinton, a grain buyer for Consolidated Grain and Barge.

"This would be the type of year you would expect to have more interest in DP contracts," he said. "We have a better crop this year than last year. With the price of grain falling, there is more of an incentive to wait to price it."

And that should not pose a tax problem as long as farmers handle the contracts properly. Husek said farmers need to sign a contract that specifies delivery and payment dates and proves no money changed hands at the time of delivery.
Husek also noted that the IRS memo has not been officially approved or published and it does not seem likely it will go into effect in time to affect 1996 taxes.
An IRS spokeswoman in Washington told Reuters on Monday the memo applies only to the case of the Washington farmer.
The National Grain and Feed Association also played down the significance of the IRS memo.
"Yes, it (the memo) is a possible problem. But it should not be blown out of proportion," said NGFA's David Barrett. "People shouldn't read more into it than it is."
And while many farmers compute AMT, few have had to pay the tax. According to U.S. Agriculture Department data, only one-half of one percent of all farmers paid AMT in 1992.
IRS allows a $40,000 exemption on AMT base income, so AMT rarely costs farmers more than regular income tax, Husek said.
